idiom_name: Promise.all / allSettled (typed) for the latch; Atomics.wait/notify + SharedArrayBuffer in workers
implementation_notes: TypeScript adds no synchronization of its own - it inherits JavaScript's single-threaded model and the worker_threads/Atomics facilities - so the realization matches JavaScript, with types along for the ride: Promise.all over a tuple preserves each element's result type, which removes the casts a hand-rolled counter collector would need, and the fan-in error path can be typed as a discriminated union. A reusable barrier is only possible inside workers: a SharedArrayBuffer viewed as Int32Array, Atomics.add to arrive and Atomics.wait/notify (or waitAsync where blocking is impossible) to release, modelled as a small class over that shared memory. Main-thread code must never block, so the promise form stays the default.
pitfalls: Structured cloning hides the sharing: a typed array that does not wrap a SharedArrayBuffer is copied into the worker, so a barrier built over a cloned buffer never rendezvous - and TypeScript's types cannot express 'this memory is shared'.
Browsers only expose SharedArrayBuffer under cross-origin isolation, so worker-thread barriers that work in Node fail to construct in a page; the latch form has no such restriction.

A timed-out Atomics.wait returns without releasing the other parties, so the caller must abort or cancel the shared group instead of proceeding as if the phase completed; Promise.all's first-rejection semantics likewise leave remaining promises running.
